meters.label: Milliseconds of CPU for the request

frames.narration: An endpoint turns a request with 10,000 fields into a hash table of 16,384 buckets, and later looks every field up again. The hash function mixes the key well and the load factor is 61%.
Keys spread over 7,520 buckets and the longest chain has 6 entries. A lookup compares 1.29 keys on average, and the whole request makes 15,968 comparisons: about 0.16 ms at an assumed 10 ns each.

Now the hash function looks only at the last decimal digit of the key. The same 10,000 keys land in 10 buckets, the longest chain has 1,027 entries, and the request makes 10,001,980 comparisons, about 100 ms.

An attacker who knows the hash function does not need luck: they compute 10,000 keys that all hash to bucket 0 and send them. One chain of 10,000, 100,000,000 comparisons, about 1 second of CPU from one request.
The fix is a hash with a secret seed picked at start-up. The same crafted keys now spread out: 16,034 comparisons and a longest chain of 5. The attacker cannot know which keys collide.

A balanced tree map avoids the question: every lookup is O(log n), about 14 comparisons for 10,000 keys, whoever chose them (roughly 3 ms for the whole request), and keys come back in order. The price is slower lookups than a hash table on honest data.
